h: Monks, Mount Stewart and the Titanic Link
p: The site has an industrial past worth a look: an old limekiln still stands, and the clay pits once dug here for brick and tile making later flooded to become part of the wetlands you walk around today, which is a nice example of industry handing land back to nature.
Time a visit for high tide if you can, when birds are pushed closer to shore and easier to see.

Strangford Lough has lots more to explore. Nendrum Monastic Site, on Mahee Island, is an atmospheric early Christian monastery with stone walls, a round tower stump and a sundial, reached by causeways across the lough. Further down the Ards Peninsula, Mount Stewart is a beautiful National Trust house with celebrated gardens, perfect for a leisurely afternoon.

Comber also has a fascinating connection to the Titanic. Thomas Andrews, the Harland and Wolff shipbuilder who led the ship's design and died in the disaster in 1912, was born in Comber, and there's a memorial hall in the town named after him. It's a poignant piece of local history.

Those brent geese have quite a journey behind them. The pale-bellied brents that winter on Strangford Lough breed in the high Arctic of Canada, flying thousands of miles to reach these shores each autumn, which makes seeing them feel all the more special. For a different way to explore, the Comber Greenway is a traffic-free walking and cycling path along an old railway line from Comber towards east Belfast, great for families on bikes. At the southern end of the lough, a little car ferry crosses the narrows between Strangford and Portaferry, a fun short trip with lovely views.
